## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sīlavīmaṁsajātaka* (Ja 362) is a birth-story in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. It has been translated into English as *A Test of Virtue* by Bhikkhu Sujato [SuttaCentral] and under the title *Virtue and Learning* by Anandajoti [Anandajoti 2010]. In the narrative framework, the Buddha delivers the teaching while staying at the Jetavana monastery regarding a brahmin who wished to test the power and comparative value of moral virtue (*sīla*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. In the past story (introduced with the verse incipit *Sīlaṁ seyyo*), the king holds the protagonist in high regard for his virtue beyond other brahmins [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. To determine whether virtue or learning is more valuable, the Bodhisatta takes a coin each day until he is arrested on the third day, thereby proving the supremacy of virtue over mere learning [SuttaCentral; Anandajoti 2010].

In discussions of the bodhisattva perfections (*pāramī*), the *Sīlavīmaṁsajātaka* is frequently cited to demonstrate the primary importance attached to morality, highlighting the Bodhisatta's conclusion that without virtue, wisdom has no worth [Narada 2008; War Yar Mein Da 2015]. Textually, the verses of the Jātaka are preserved alongside its commentary in the edition of V. Fausböll [Fausböll 1883]. DharmaNexus aligns the text internally with two passages in the third volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (matching up to 487 characters) [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four modern translations of the text in four languages [SuttaCentral].
